avoid.reason: Caution in Overtown and Liberty City; watch for theft/scams in South Beach nightlife

hood_desc: South Beach is the iconic Art Deco beachfront of white sand, Ocean Drive nightlife, glamorous hotels and people-watching, ideal for partygoers, beach lovers and first-time visitors.
Wynwood is Miami's edgy arts district famous for the Wynwood Walls murals, breweries, galleries and hip eateries, perfect for creatives, foodies and young travelers.
Little Havana is the vibrant Cuban heart of Miami along Calle Ocho, with cigar shops, salsa, domino parks and authentic food, great for culture seekers and lively atmosphere.
Brickell is the sleek downtown financial district of high-rise condos, rooftop bars and upscale dining, suited to business travelers and those wanting a modern urban base.
Coconut Grove is a lush, laid-back bayfront village of leafy streets, sidewalk cafes, marinas and boutiques, appealing to families and travelers seeking a relaxed, upscale vibe.

water.note: Tap water is treated and safe to drink.

transit.pay: Tap a contactless credit/debit card or phone straight at Metrorail faregates and bus readers ($2.25 a ride), or buy an EASY Card (about $2) from station vending machines; the GO Miami-Dade app sells mobile tickets too. The downtown Metromover is completely free. Brightline and Tri-Rail sell their own tickets via app or station machines.
transit.hours: Metrorail and Metromover run daily from about 5am to midnight; a handful of Metrobus routes run 24 hours.

food.name: Cuban sandwich
food.desc: Roast pork, ham, Swiss, pickles and mustard pressed in lard-brushed Cuban bread until the crust shatters. Miami's single most essential bite.

places.name: Sanguich de Miami
places.note: Michelin Bib Gourmand; two-day marinated pork, week-brined ham and house-baked bread. Widely called the city's best.

places.name: Versailles Restaurant
places.note: The world's most famous Cuban restaurant since 1971; the double-press technique crisps the honey-glazed ham.

places.name: El Palacio de los Jugos
places.note: Chaotic open-air market stall with mojo pork piled high; cheap, messy and deeply local.

food.name: Stone crab claws
food.desc: Sweet claws served chilled with mustard sauce, harvested off Florida in season from mid-October to early May. Invented as a dish right here in 1921.

places.name: Joe's Stone Crab
places.note: The 1913 original that created the dish; no reservations, so queue early or use Joe's Take Away next door.

places.name: Garcia's Seafood Grille and Fish Market
places.note: Family-run waterfront fish house with old-Miami atmosphere and far shorter waits than Joe's.

places.name: Monty's Raw Bar
places.note: Marina-side raw bar for claws with a rum drink and live music; casual and open late.

food.name: Croquetas de jamon
food.desc: Crisp-fried logs of silky ham bechamel, eaten by the handful at bakery counters and ventanitas all day long.

places.name: Islas Canarias Restaurant
places.note: Legendary croquetas, crunchy outside and creamy within; a local favourite for decades.

places.name: Sergio's
places.note: Chunky filling that actually tastes of ham; the chain has served over 20 million croquetas.

places.name: La Casita
places.note: Classic sit-down Cuban with rich, perfectly breaded ham croquetas and strong cafecito.

food.name: Pastelitos de guayaba
food.desc: Flaky glazed puff pastry filled with guava, often with cream cheese. Grab a box for a dollar or two at any Cuban bakery.

places.name: Karla Bakery
places.note: Hialeah favourite with oozing guava-and-cheese pastelitos and a full Cuban breakfast counter.

places.name: Ricky Bakery
places.note: Tops The Infatuation's pastelito rankings for the balance of tangy cream cheese and guava.

places.name: Pinecrest Bakery
places.note: Praised for defined, book-page layers of puff pastry; many branches open 24 hours.

food.name: Haitian griot
food.desc: Marinated pork shoulder braised then fried crisp, served with pikliz, rice and beans. Miami has the largest Haitian community in the US.

places.name: Chez Le Bebe
places.note: Griot specialist since the 1980s: fatty fried pork chunks with rice, salad and pork jus for dipping.

places.name: Naomi's Garden Restaurant and Lounge
places.note: Leafy courtyard for griot, oxtail and fried snapper, with live music on weekends.

places.name: Chef Creole
places.note: Reliable takeout counter for griot, conch and fried fish; a long-running local institution.

food.name: Ceviche and Peruvian seafood
food.desc: Lime-cured fish with leche de tigre, sweet potato and choclo. Miami's Peruvian community makes it a genuine local specialty.

places.name: CVI.CHE 105
places.note: Chef Juan Chipoco's flagship; huge ceviche list plus tiradito and lomo saltado in a lively room.

places.name: Ceviches by Divino
places.note: Neighbourhood Peruvian gastropub with bright ceviches and generous portions at fair prices.

food.name: Cafecito and colada
food.desc: Tiny, syrup-sweet shots of Cuban espresso, or a colada shared out in thimble cups with strangers at a walk-up window.

places.name: Versailles Ventanita
places.note: The unofficial town square of Cuban Miami; strong, sweet, perfectly foamed cafecito and endless politics.

places.name: La Carreta
places.note: Open very late, with coladas built for sharing around the group.

places.name: La Colada Gourmet
places.note: Roasts daily and runs a long list of creative cafecito variations; a modern take on the ventanita.

food.name: Mojito
food.desc: White rum, lime, sugar cane and a thicket of fresh mint. Miami's Cuban bar culture treats it as a craft, not a poolside cliche.

places.name: Cafe La Trova
places.note: Julio Cabrera's cantinero-style bar, repeatedly ranked among North America's best; showmanship and precision.

places.name: Ball and Chain
places.note: Restored 1930s jazz club with a pineapple stage, live son and salsa, and a reader-voted best mojito.

landmarks: Vizcaya Museum and Gardens
A stunning early-20th-century Italian Renaissance-style villa on Biscayne Bay with formal gardens, making it one of Miami's most photogenic historic estates.
Ocean Drive & Art Deco Historic District
Pastel-colored Art Deco hotels lining South Beach make this strip one of the most photographed streetscapes in the U.S.
Freedom Tower
A landmark 1925 Mediterranean Revival tower and National Historic Landmark that symbolizes Miami's Cuban immigrant history.
Wynwood Walls
An outdoor street-art museum packed with vivid murals by world-renowned artists, a favorite backdrop for colorful photos.
Bayside Marketplace
A lively waterfront shopping and dining complex in Downtown Miami offering skyline and marina views.
Little Havana (Calle Ocho)
The heart of Miami's Cuban-American culture, famous for cigar shops, domino players, and colorful murals along SW 8th Street.
Coral Castle
A mysterious limestone sculpture garden built by one man, prized by photographers for its oddity and dramatic megalithic carvings.
South Beach
Miami's iconic stretch of white sand and turquoise water framed by Art Deco skyline views and lifeguard towers.
Bayfront Park
A downtown green space along Biscayne Bay offering sweeping views of the Miami skyline and Freedom Tower.
Miami Beach (Lummus Park)
The classic Miami postcard shot combining beach, palm trees, and Ocean Drive's neon-lit Art Deco hotels.

train.note: No international trains from Florida. Amtrak's Silver Meteor (to New York) and Floridian (to Chicago) depart from Miami's Amtrak station at Hialeah, northwest of downtown, and both are overnight services with sleeping cars. High-speed Brightline trains run from the separate MiamiCentral terminal downtown to Fort Lauderdale, West Palm Beach and Orlando International Airport in about three and a half hours, and are far quicker and more frequent than Amtrak for those city pairs. Tri-Rail commuter trains also link Miami with Fort Lauderdale and West Palm Beach on the Amtrak corridor.

bus.note: No international coach routes - Florida is a peninsula and everything beyond it goes by air or sea. Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/) and FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) link Miami with cities across the US, and RedCoach (https://www.redcoachusa.com/) runs premium coaches with reclining seats to Orlando, Tampa, Gainesville and the rest of Florida. Typical times are around four hours to Orlando and two to Fort Myers or Key West-bound connections. Book online; several operators load curbside rather than at a staffed terminal.

intl.to: Bimini & Freeport, Grand Bahama (Bahamas) - departs Port Everglades, Fort Lauderdale

ferry.note: The Bahamas fast ferry actually sails from Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale, about 30 miles north of downtown Miami - allow an hour to get there and bring your passport, since this is a full international departure with immigration formalities. The crossing to Bimini takes roughly two hours. PortMiami itself handles cruise ships, not scheduled ferries, and sailings can be cancelled in rough weather or during hurricane season.

half.name: Everglades National Park
half.blurb: Vast sawgrass wilderness where airboats glide past alligators, wading birds and endless subtropical marsh horizons.

half.name: Key Largo (John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park)
half.blurb: Gateway to the Keys with turquoise waters, living coral reefs and superb snorkeling and diving.

half.name: Fort Lauderdale
half.blurb: Breezy coastal city of palm-lined beaches, canal cruises and the lively Las Olas Boulevard.

half.name: Biscayne National Park
half.blurb: Mostly-underwater marine park protecting mangroves, clear bays and coral reefs teeming with tropical fish.

half.name: Islamorada
half.blurb: Laid-back island village famous for sport fishing, tarpon feeding and mellow waterfront seafood shacks.

half.name: Naples
half.blurb: Upscale Gulf Coast town with white-sand beaches, a scenic pier and refined shopping streets.
